pages.text:
*Way to Lose #25: Get so used to losing that winning feels like a mistake.*

The Sunnyvale Sprouts are the only team below us, and they look terrified. I am not. I am vibrating like a phone on a table. My cleats, one green lace and one orange, dig into the slanted turf. Coach Gin stands before us in her fluorescent windbreaker, holding her thermos like a gavel. She does not yell or draw Xs and Os. Instead, she looks at the duck pond behind our goal, where a single mallard is preening a feather with intense focus.

"Look. Pass. Trust. Duck," she says.

That is it. No pep talk. No "leave it all on the field." Just four words that make no sense together. I blink. I look at Tank, who is still holding his gloves. I look at Josie, whose mouth is slightly open.

"Duck?" Josie asks.

"The bird," Gin says, sipping her tea. "It is there. Do not kick it."

The whistle blows. I step onto the pitch. The grass is wet, and the air smells like cut hay and fear. I take the ball at midfield. I look left, then right. For the first time, I do not look for the applause. I look for the gap.
pages.image: A bright yellow coach in a windbreaker points toward a muddy soccer field where a single mallard stands near the goal; a wiry girl with a high ponytail and yellow armband watches the duck intently while other players look confused.

pages.text:
Half-time is a mystery. The score is zero to zero, a number so rare for the Mud Hens that it feels like holding your breath underwater and forgetting to breathe.

But things are different. Ahmed, the fastest kid who hates passing, is standing in the midfield. He is not running. He is waiting. When a Sprout player comes at him, he does not sprint. He drops his shoulder and passes to Tank. Tank does not apologize. He just takes the ball and clears it with a heavy, gentle thud.

The twins, Leo and Mateo, are on the left side. They are not arguing about who is older. They are taking turns holding the line. One steps up, the other drops back. It looks like they are dancing, except there is no music and everyone is sweating.

Priya is in goal. Her glasses are strapped tight. Her eyes are open. All of them. She is not flinching. She is watching the angle. I watch her, and my heart does a weird flip, like a coin landing on its edge.

"Zero to zero," Josie whispers to me. "Do you feel that?"

"I feel like I forgot how to lose," I say. And that is the scariest part.
pages.image: A small girl in oversized goalkeeper gloves stands alert with eyes wide open, watching a soccer ball approach; a large gentle boy in a red jersey clears the ball with his foot while two identical boys take turns marking opponents on the muddy slanted field.

pages.text:
Second half. Minute twelve. Ahmed has the ball at the edge of the box, looking my way with that "I am not running" expression. He sends it low, cutting across the wet grass like a hockey puck on ice. I am there before I even decide to be. I strike it without thinking, my cleats finding the wet turf with a solid thud.

The ball zips past the Sprout goalie, who is still staring at Ahmed. It hits the net. It goes in.

The park explodes. Not a cheer, exactly. More like a roar. The ducks in the pond quack in genuine surprise. One to zero.

Then, minute twenty, they score. A header. Ugly. Lucky. One to one.

Minute twenty-four. Josie gets the ball on the wing. She kicks it hard, but it hits her own shoulder first. The ball bounces off the crossbar, hangs in the air for a split second, and drops into the net.

The ref looks at the ball, then at Josie, then at his watch. He signals for the goal. Two to one.

Josie is screaming. Tank is hugging her. I am standing still, my hands in my pockets, feeling the vibration of the crowd through the soles of my shoes. We are winning. Actually winning.
pages.image: A soccer ball bounces off a player's shoulder and flies into the net; a referee in black stripes raises his arms to signal a goal; a wiry girl with a yellow armband stands still with hands in pockets, watching the chaotic celebration around her.

pages.text:
The final whistle blows. It is not a sound. It is a physical force that hits my chest and pushes the air out of my lungs.

Tank, who is the size of a refrigerator, picks me up. He lifts me off the ground, and I kick my legs in the air like a happy dog. I cannot breathe, but I do not want to land.

My dad is on the sideline. His foam finger is moving so fast it is a blur, a helicopter of support. He is shouting something, but I can only hear the rhythm of his voice.

Abuela stands up from her folding chair. She does not stand up slowly. She launches. Her arms go up. Her mouth opens, and a sound comes out that I have never heard from her before. It is not a word. It is a roar. It carries across the parking lot. It probably carries across three counties.

Luz is on the ground, cross-legged. She is writing in her crayon notebook. She holds up the page. It says "WIN" in gold, the letters shaky and thick. Below it, she has drawn a duck. The duck has a crown.

I am still in the air. I am looking at the sky. For the first time, the scoreboard is not the only thing that matters. Or maybe it is. I don't know. I just know I am flying.
pages.image: A large gentle boy lifts a smiling wiry girl into the air; a man waves a blurry foam finger; a small girl holds up a drawing of a crowned duck; a sharp-eyed grandmother stands with arms raised, shouting, on the sideline of a muddy soccer field.

pages.text:
My phone buzzes, then again, and again.

I check the screen. Carter Boyle has posted a video. It is not the own goal. It shows my shot, the net rippling, and the roar. The title reads "MUD HENS WIN!!" with that happy trombone sound from cartoons playing underneath.

Streetlights flicker on outside, casting long orange shadows over the houses. Everyone will know by Monday. The hallway will be buzzing. I am the girl who scored. I am the captain who led us to our first win.

I feel light, and I feel solid. I feel exactly who I have always thought I would be.

I do not notice that this feeling is being lent to me by everyone else. I just keep watching the video, smiling, letting the phone vibrate against my palm. To me, this is what it feels like to be enough.
pages.image: A girl with a high ponytail sits in a car passenger seat, looking at her phone screen which shows a soccer goal; the car window is open with streetlights glowing in the background; she smiles with a mix of pride and quiet uncertainty.
